newsitem.title: UK: LME zinc performs strongly while copper fades.
newsitem.headline: LME zinc performs strongly while copper fades.

text.p: Zinc prices were lifted to new giddy heights and the nearby backwardation flared on Wednesday as tightness in the autumn months made itself felt.
The other metals played second fiddle to stubbornly buoyant zinc, which finished near its new seven-year highs at $1,553 per tonne, up $9 from Tuesday's kerb close.
Zinc's backwardation shot out to a high of $20/$25 in the afternoon rings, from level on Tuesday, reflecting tightness starting in the September dates.
It finally ended the kerb just narrower around $17.
Traders said Far Eastern borrowing and short covering, along with good consumer demand, was boosting zinc despite the market being very overbought on the charts.
Far Eastern shorts and a big European merchants are thought to be engaged in a tug of war over the zinc price, which has climbed steadily since the start of the year. The next target was $1,600.
In sharp contrast three months copper flagged in thin volumes and settled $27 slower at $2,273.
Cash/threes backwardation shrank to $60/$65, compared to $100 on Tuesday and a peak of $270 last week as one of the last dates in two weeks of tightness dropped off.
"It's all going to be over on July 25," a trader said, adding that more metal attracted by the recent backwardation was expected to come into LME warehouses in coming days.
Stocks rose by 5,000 tonnes on Wednesday, bringing the total to 200,950 tonnes.

But the flagship metal's woes did not carry over into aluminium, which took on a more bullish stance after speculative and trade buying pushed it over the $1,620 resistance area in early trading. Prices ended $27 higher at $1,642.
Aluminium was helped by tightness emerging in September dates and good borrowing of the August/September spread. The cash/threes contango shrank to around $11 against $20 on Tuesday afternoon.
With reported stocks dropping steadily, shorts may have to scramble and pay higher prices to cover in coming months than they may have thought previously, analysts said.
Tin settled unchanged at $5,370, but lead popped up by $5 to end at $650, boosted by stronger zinc.
Nickel was also a touch firmer at $6,780, up by $15.
Alloy ticked higher with primary aluminium and was last indicated at $1,465/$1,470.
